name: Americana from Mount
description: Master the Americana from Mount in BJJ. Step-by-step shoulder lock execution with grip details. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Americana from Mount represents one of the most fundamental shoulder lock submissions in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, combining positional dominance with joint manipulation to force the tap. Executed from the mount position, this technique targets the shoulder's rotational limit by painting the opponent's wrist toward the mat while maintaining elbow control, creating a figure-four grip that generates enormous rotational pressure on the glenohumeral joint.

Strategically, the Americana functions as both a finishing submission and a positional control tool. When opponents defend by keeping their elbows tight to their body, they create the exact arm positioning needed for the Americana setup. This creates a powerful dilemma: defend the mount by framing and risk armbar attacks, or keep arms close and become vulnerable to the Americana. Advanced practitioners chain the Americana with straight armbars and Kimuras, using each submission threat to open opportunities for the others.

The mechanical efficiency of the Americana makes it particularly effective from mount because gravity assists the attack. Your body weight pins the opponent's shoulder while both hands work together to rotate the arm past its natural range of motion. Unlike submissions requiring speed or explosive movement, the Americana rewards patient, incremental pressure that gradually compromises the joint until the opponent must submit or face serious injury.
key_principles: Maintain heavy chest pressure on opponent's shoulder throughout the submission to prevent hitchhiker escape and bridge attempts
Control the elbow position first before attacking the wrist—the elbow must stay below shoulder level for the submission to work
Use figure-four grip configuration with your wrist behind their wrist and your other hand gripping your own wrist for maximum leverage
Paint the wrist toward the mat in an arcing motion rather than pushing directly down, creating rotational torque on the shoulder joint
Keep your elbows tight to your body during the finish to prevent opponent from straightening their arm and escaping
Apply pressure gradually and consistently rather than explosively, allowing training partners time to tap safely
Sprawl your hips back slightly during the finish to add downward pressure on their elbow while painting the wrist
setup_requirements: Established mount position with stable base and weight distributed through hips onto opponent's torso
Opponent's arm isolated with elbow bent at approximately 90 degrees and positioned below shoulder level
Control of opponent's wrist with your same-side hand, thumb pointing toward their fingers
Your opposite hand threaded under their tricep, ready to establish figure-four grip
Opponent's shoulder pinned to mat by your chest pressure, preventing them from turning into the attack
Clear space to paint opponent's wrist toward the mat without obstruction from their other arm

execution_steps.description: From mount, identify the target arm—typically the one opponent uses to frame against your hip. Push their elbow to the mat and trap it between your hip and their body, ensuring the elbow stays bent and below shoulder level.
execution_steps.timing: Opportunistic—wait for opponent to frame or push

execution_steps.description: Grip their wrist with your same-side hand (right hand to their right wrist), keeping your thumb pointing toward their fingers. Pin the wrist to the mat near their head while maintaining chest pressure on their shoulder.
Slide your opposite hand under their tricep from the outside, reaching toward your wrist-gripping hand. Your arm should pass behind their elbow, with your forearm pressing against their tricep.
execution_steps.timing: Maintain constant wrist pressure while threading

execution_steps.description: Grip your own wrist with your threading hand, creating a figure-four lock. Your wrist should be directly behind their wrist, and your other hand grips your wrist palm-to-palm or with an S-grip for maximum control.
execution_steps.timing: Quick connection to prevent arm extraction

execution_steps.description: Adjust your chest pressure to pin their shoulder firmly to the mat. Keep your elbows tight to your body. Sprawl your hips back slightly to add downward pressure on their trapped elbow while maintaining mount stability.
execution_steps.timing: Settle position before applying submission pressure

execution_steps.description: Lift their elbow slightly off the mat while simultaneously painting their wrist in an arc toward their hip. The motion creates rotational pressure on the shoulder joint. Apply gradually increasing pressure until opponent taps or you feel the joint approaching its limit.

common_counters.counter: Hitchhiker escape—opponent straightens arm and rotates toward the trapped side
common_counters.your_response: Maintain heavy chest pressure on shoulder and keep their elbow pinned below shoulder level; if they begin rotating, transition to armbar by stepping over their head

common_counters.counter: Bridge and roll toward trapped arm side to relieve pressure
common_counters.your_response: Post your free hand on the mat toward the roll direction; if they succeed in rolling, maintain grip and finish Americana from side control or transition to Kimura

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs their own collar or belt to anchor the arm
common_counters.your_response: Strip the grip by sliding your wrist-control hand down to break their fingers off; alternatively, switch to cross collar choke while they focus on grip fighting

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens arm completely to prevent figure-four
common_counters.your_response: Immediately transition to straight armbar by stepping over their face; their extended arm is perfectly positioned for the armbar attack

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent's elbow to rise above shoulder level during setup
common_errors.consequence: Submission becomes ineffective as shoulder rotation is not compromised; opponent easily extracts arm
common_errors.correction: Pin elbow to mat using hip pressure before attacking wrist; maintain constant downward pressure on elbow throughout the technique

common_errors.error: Applying explosive, jerking pressure during the finish
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious shoulder injury to training partner; also telegraphs the submission allowing escape
common_errors.correction: Apply slow, steady rotational pressure in a controlled arc; give partner time to tap and always release immediately upon submission

common_errors.error: Losing chest pressure on shoulder while focusing on arm manipulation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent turns into attack, extracts arm, or executes hitchhiker escape
common_errors.correction: Maintain heavy chest-to-shoulder contact throughout; your torso pins their shoulder while arms control the joint

common_errors.error: Pushing wrist straight down toward mat instead of painting in an arc
common_errors.consequence: Minimal rotational pressure on shoulder; opponent can resist with arm strength alone
common_errors.correction: Paint wrist in an arc toward their hip while lifting elbow slightly; the circular motion creates the rotational torque that compromises the joint

common_errors.error: Sitting upright during the submission attempt
common_errors.consequence: Reduces pressure, allows opponent to bridge and roll, exposes you to sweep attempts
common_errors.correction: Stay low with chest heavy on opponent; sprawl hips back during finish to add pressure while maintaining base

common_errors.error: Failing to control both wrist and elbow simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Opponent straightens arm to escape figure-four or rotates elbow up to relieve pressure
common_errors.correction: Figure-four grip must control wrist while your arm behind their tricep controls elbow position; both control points work together

training_progressions.description: Practice figure-four grip configuration in isolation. Partner lies still while you establish and maintain the grip from mount. Focus on wrist-behind-wrist positioning and comfortable grip that allows sustained control. Drill grip entry from both sides.

Combine grip mechanics with mount maintenance. Partner provides light frames and movement while you maintain mount and establish Americana grips without finishing. Focus on recognizing when opponent's arm is positioned for the attack and transitioning smoothly from control to submission setup.

Practice complete submission sequence with partner defending at 50% intensity. Focus on the painting arc motion and proper elbow control during the finish. Drill transitioning to armbar when opponent straightens arm and to Kimura when they turn toward trapped side.

Incorporate Americana attacks into positional sparring from mount. Partner defends with full resistance. Focus on chaining with other mount attacks, timing entries against defensive movements, and recognizing when to abandon the attack and maintain position instead.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of painting toward opponent's hip, drive their wrist in an arc toward the mat above their head, as if painting a fence. Creates different rotational angle that can be effective when standard direction is blocked.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent blocks the standard painting direction toward their hip or when their arm is positioned higher near their head

variants_and_adaptations.description: Same figure-four grip mechanics applied from side control position. Requires heavy crossface pressure to prevent escape. Often accessed when mount is unstable or opponent is defending aggressively.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When transitioning from mount to side control during opponent's escape attempt or when mount feels unstable

variants_and_adaptations.description: Applied from standing position or top turtle using same grip configuration. Requires different body positioning to generate pressure without mount. Common in wrestling and catch wrestling contexts.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: During scrambles or when opponent turtles and exposes their arm

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of the Americana from Mount?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to apply rotational pressure to the opponent's shoulder joint by painting their wrist toward the mat while controlling their elbow in a bent position below shoulder level. This creates a submission that forces the tap by threatening to dislocate or hyperrotate the shoulder. Secondary goals include maintaining mount position and creating openings for other attacks when opponent defends.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Americana from Mount from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The technique starts from any mount variation including standard mount, low mount, high mount, 3-4 mount, or technical mount. The key requirement is having stable top position with opponent on their back and your weight controlling their torso. The most common setup occurs from low or standard mount when opponent frames against your hips with bent arms.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Americana from Mount?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Americana requires a figure-four grip configuration: your same-side hand grips opponent's wrist with thumb pointing toward their fingers, while your opposite hand threads under their tricep and grips your own wrist. The grip creates a locked system where your wrist is behind their wrist and your forearm controls their elbow position. Palm-to-palm or S-grip connections are both effective.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you counter the hitchhiker escape when opponent begins straightening and rotating?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent initiates the hitchhiker escape by straightening their arm and rotating toward the trapped side, you have two primary responses. First, maintain heavy chest pressure on their shoulder and drive their elbow back down below shoulder level to reset the Americana. Second, if their arm is already extending, immediately transition to armbar by stepping your leg over their face while maintaining wrist control. Their straightening arm creates the exact position needed for the armbar finish.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the optimal time to attempt Americana from Mount?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when opponent frames against your hips or chest with a bent arm, creating the elbow-below-shoulder position naturally. Other high-percentage moments include when opponent attempts to push your hips back to create escape space, when they reach across their body to prevent choke attempts, or immediately after defending an armbar attempt when their arm returns to a bent defensive position. Avoid attempting when opponent's arms are extended or positioned above shoulder level.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent posts their hand on your hip to create space—how do you transition to Americana?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent posts on your hip, their elbow is typically bent and positioned perfectly for Americana. Immediately pin their wrist to the mat by driving it toward their head while dropping your chest onto their shoulder. Slide your opposite hand under their now-trapped tricep and establish the figure-four grip. Their own framing attempt created the bent-arm position you need. The key is speed—capture the wrist before they can withdraw the arm.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most critical mechanical detail for finishing the Americana?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most critical detail is the painting arc motion combined with slight elbow elevation. Rather than pushing the wrist straight down, you must lift their elbow slightly off the mat while simultaneously painting their wrist in an arc toward their hip. This circular motion creates rotational torque on the shoulder joint that cannot be resisted through arm strength alone. Without this arc, opponents can often muscle through the submission using their bicep strength.

knowledge_assessment.question: What direction of force creates the submission pressure in the Americana?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The submission pressure comes from rotational force on the shoulder joint, not direct downward pressure. The figure-four grip creates a lever system where lifting the elbow while painting the wrist generates internal rotation of the humerus past the shoulder's comfortable range. The force vectors are: wrist moves toward opponent's hip in an arc, elbow lifts slightly off mat, and your chest pins their shoulder to prevent them from rotating with the pressure. All three elements must work together.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the Americana chain with armbar attacks from mount?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Americana and armbar create a powerful attacking dilemma from mount. When opponent bends their arm to defend the armbar, they create the exact position needed for Americana. When they straighten their arm to escape the Americana (particularly the hitchhiker escape), they expose themselves to the armbar. To chain effectively: if opponent straightens during Americana attempt, immediately step over their face maintaining wrist control and transition to armbar. If they re-bend to escape armbar, return to Americana. This cycling continues until you finish or they exhaust themselves.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent grabs their own belt to anchor their arm against your Americana—what is your response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent anchors by gripping their belt or gi, you have several responses. First, attempt to strip the grip by sliding your wrist-control hand down to pry their fingers off the belt. Second, if the grip is strong, transition to a cross collar choke since their focus on grip fighting leaves their neck exposed. Third, switch to Kimura grip by releasing the figure-four and controlling their wrist with both hands, then work to break the anchor grip with superior leverage. Fourth, abandon the submission temporarily and use your positional advantage to set up a different attack, returning to the Americana when they release the grip.

safety_considerations: The Americana attacks the shoulder joint through rotational pressure and can cause serious injury including shoulder dislocation, rotator cuff tears, and ligament damage if applied too quickly or without control. Always apply the painting arc motion gradually, giving your training partner ample time to recognize the submission and tap. Never use explosive or jerking motions during the finish. Release immediately upon feeling a tap or hearing a verbal submission. During drilling, communicate with your partner about pressure levels and stop well before the joint reaches its end range. Practitioners with previous shoulder injuries should approach this technique carefully and inform training partners of any limitations. In competition, be aware that the Americana can cause injury even after an opponent taps if you continue applying pressure during the release—always maintain control and release smoothly.
position_integration: The Americana from Mount functions as a cornerstone submission within the mount attacking system, integrating seamlessly with armbars, cross collar chokes, and Ezekiel chokes. From mount, when opponents keep their elbows tight to defend collar chokes and armbars, they inadvertently create the bent-arm position needed for Americana attacks. Conversely, when they straighten their arms to escape the Americana, they expose themselves to armbar attacks. This creates a continuous attacking cycle where each defense opens another submission threat. The Americana also serves as a position-maintenance tool: even unsuccessful attempts force opponents to expend energy defending while you remain in mount. When the Americana fails completely, you typically maintain mount position with minimal loss. The technique chains forward into Kimura attacks when opponents turn toward the trapped side and backward into mount retention when they successfully escape the initial grip. Understanding this integration allows practitioners to flow between attacks based on opponent reactions rather than forcing isolated submission attempts.
